questions.text: Which statement about a candidate key is TRUE?

options.text: There can be only one per relation
It must be a single attribute

questions.solution: A candidate key uniquely identifies a tuple and no proper subset of it does — that is what minimal means. A relation may have several candidate keys, one of which is chosen as the primary key. Only the primary key is forbidden NULLs.

questions.text: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies A → B, B → C and C → D. Which are TRUE?

options.text: The closure of A is {A, B, C, D}

questions.solution: A<sup>+</sup> = {A, B, C, D}, so A determines every attribute and is a candidate key, and A → D follows by transitivity. B<sup>+</sup> = {B, C, D} omits A, so B is not a candidate key.

questions.text: A relation is in 2NF but not 3NF. What must be true?

options.text: It has a transitive dependency on a non-prime attribute

questions.solution: 2NF removes partial dependencies, so those are already gone. 3NF additionally forbids a non-prime attribute depending on another non-prime attribute — a transitive dependency. Multivalued dependencies belong to 4NF.

questions.text: What is the difference between 3NF and BCNF?

options.text: BCNF requires every determinant to be a superkey

questions.solution: BCNF demands that for every non-trivial X → Y, X is a superkey. 3NF makes an exception when Y is a prime attribute, which is why every BCNF relation is in 3NF but not conversely. BCNF decomposition can also fail to be dependency-preserving.

questions.text: A relation violates 1NF when:

options.text: It has a composite primary key
An attribute holds a multivalued or composite value
It has more than one candidate key

questions.solution: 1NF requires every attribute value to be atomic. Storing a list of phone numbers in one cell breaks it. Composite keys, transitive dependencies and multiple candidate keys are all perfectly compatible with 1NF.

questions.text: Which ACID property guarantees that a committed transaction survives a system crash?
questions.solution: Durability means committed changes are permanent, normally achieved by write-ahead logging to stable storage before commit is acknowledged. Atomicity is all-or-nothing, isolation concerns concurrent visibility.

questions.text: Which anomalies can occur under the READ COMMITTED isolation level?
questions.solution: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads by only showing committed data, but a row can change between two reads (non-repeatable read), new rows can appear (phantom), and concurrent updates can overwrite one another. SERIALIZABLE prevents all four.

questions.text: What does SELECT COUNT(*) return compared with SELECT COUNT(column)?

options.text: COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs in that column
COUNT(column) counts all rows; COUNT(*) skips NULLs

questions.solution: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of content. COUNT(column) counts only rows where that column is not NULL. This is the most common source of unexpected aggregate results.

questions.text: Relation R has 5 tuples and relation S has 3 tuples. How many tuples are in R CROSS JOIN S?
questions.solution: A cross join (Cartesian product) pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S, giving 5 × 3 = 15. Any join condition then filters this set down.

questions.text: R has 10 tuples and S has 6 tuples, joined on a common attribute. What is the maximum possible number of tuples in a NATURAL JOIN of R and S?
questions.solution: In the extreme case every tuple of R matches every tuple of S — when the join attribute holds the same value throughout both relations — giving 10 × 6 = 60. The minimum is 0 if nothing matches.

questions.text: Which relational algebra operator removes duplicate tuples by definition?
questions.solution: Relational algebra works on sets, so projection eliminates the duplicates that dropping columns creates. SQL is bag-based and keeps duplicates unless you write SELECT DISTINCT — a classic difference between the theory and the language.

questions.text: A weak entity set is characterised by:

options.text: Having no key of its own, depending on an owner entity
Being derived from a strong entity

questions.solution: A weak entity cannot be identified by its own attributes alone. It has a partial (discriminator) key that becomes unique only when combined with the owner's primary key, and it participates totally in the identifying relationship.

questions.text: Which indexing structure is better suited to range queries such as WHERE age BETWEEN 20 AND 30?

options.text: Bitmap index on a high-cardinality column

questions.solution: A B+ tree keeps keys in sorted order and links the leaves, so a range scan finds the start and walks forward. A hash index scatters keys deliberately, making it excellent for equality and useless for ranges.

questions.text: Why do database systems favour B+ trees over binary search trees for indexes on disk?

options.text: High fan-out means fewer disk accesses per lookup
B+ trees do not need balancing
Binary search trees cannot store duplicates

questions.solution: A single B+ tree node fills a disk block and holds hundreds of keys, so the tree is only three or four levels deep for millions of records. A binary tree of the same size would be about twenty levels — twenty disk seeks instead of four.

questions.text: Two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees which property?
questions.solution: 2PL — all locks acquired before any is released — guarantees a conflict-serialisable schedule. It does not prevent deadlock; that is why databases also run deadlock detection and abort a victim. Strict 2PL is what adds recoverability.

questions.text: Which anomalies does normalisation aim to remove from a poorly designed relation?
questions.solution: Redundancy causes the first three: you cannot record a fact without unrelated data, deleting a row loses unrelated facts, and one change must be repeated in many places. Concurrency anomalies come from interleaved transactions and are handled by isolation, not normalisation.

questions.text: Which SQL command is DDL rather than DML?
questions.solution: TRUNCATE removes all rows by deallocating the data pages, is DDL, and auto-commits — it cannot generally be rolled back. DELETE is DML, logs each row and can be rolled back.

questions.text: R(A, B, C, D, E) has FDs A → B, BC → D and E → C. How many attributes are in the closure of {A, E}?
questions.solution: Start {A, E}. A → B adds B: {A, B, E}. E → C adds C: {A, B, C, E}. Now BC → D applies, adding D: {A, B, C, D, E}. All 5 attributes, so AE is a candidate key.

questions.text: In write-ahead logging, what must happen before a modified page is written to disk?

options.text: The corresponding log record must reach stable storage
The page must be locked exclusively forever

questions.solution: The WAL rule is that the log record describing a change is forced to disk before the data page is. Without it, a crash could leave a changed page with no log entry to undo it, making recovery impossible.

questions.text: Changing the physical storage of a table without altering application programs is an example of:
questions.solution: Physical data independence isolates the conceptual schema from storage decisions such as file organisation or indexing. Logical data independence — insulating applications from conceptual schema changes — is the harder of the two to achieve.

questions.text: R(A, B, C) has functional dependencies AB → C and C → A. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
questions.solution: The candidate keys are AB and BC, so A, B and C are all prime attributes. C → A has a left side that is not a superkey, which breaks BCNF. But 3NF also allows a dependency whose right side is a prime attribute, and A is prime, so 3NF holds.

questions.text: A relation is in 2NF when it is in 1NF and:

options.text: no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key

questions.solution: 2NF removes partial dependencies. Option B describes 3NF, C describes BCNF and D describes 4NF. Note a relation whose every candidate key is a single attribute is automatically in 2NF, since no proper subset of a key exists.

questions.text: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on the key?
questions.solution: 3NF forbids a non-prime attribute determined by another non-prime attribute. The classic case is a key determining a department, which in turn determines its location, so the location depends on the key only indirectly.

questions.text: R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies A → B, B → C and C → D. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.solution: The closure of A is ABCD, so A is a key. No other attribute or combination determines A — nothing has A on its right side — so A must appear in every key, and A alone already suffices. Exactly one candidate key.

questions.text: Which statement about decomposing into BCNF is TRUE?

options.text: It is always possible while preserving all dependencies
It is always possible losslessly, but the decomposition may not preserve all dependencies
It is impossible for relations with more than three attributes
It always requires exactly two resulting relations

questions.solution: A lossless BCNF decomposition always exists, but some dependency may end up spanning two relations and become uncheckable without a join. 3NF is the compromise: it can always be reached both losslessly and dependency-preserving, which is why it is often where designs stop.

questions.text: Which normal form deals with multivalued dependencies?
questions.solution: 4NF removes non-trivial multivalued dependencies, where two independent multi-valued facts about the same key are stored together and force a cross-product of rows. Everything up to BCNF concerns functional dependencies only.

questions.text: R(A, B, C, D, E) has functional dependencies AB → C, C → D and D → E. How many attributes are in the closure of {A, B}?
questions.solution: Start with AB. AB → C adds C, then C → D adds D, then D → E adds E, giving ABCDE. All five, so AB is a candidate key.

questions.text: R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies AB → CD and D → A. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.solution: AB is a key since its closure is ABCD. Because D → A, the set BD also determines A, then AB gives C and D, so BD is a second key. B appears in both — nothing determines B, so it must be in every key. The candidate keys are AB and BD.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT one of Armstrong's three axioms?
questions.solution: The axioms are reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity, and they are sound and complete on their own. Union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity are convenient rules derived from them, not primitives.

questions.text: A functional dependency X → Y is called trivial when:

options.text: Y is a subset of X

questions.solution: If Y is contained in X the dependency holds in every possible relation and says nothing. This is why normal form definitions exempt trivial dependencies — otherwise no relation could ever satisfy them.

questions.text: An attribute is called prime when:

options.text: it appears in the primary key
it appears in at least one candidate key
it is functionally determined by every other attribute

questions.solution: Prime means part of some candidate key, not specifically the primary key that was chosen. The distinction matters directly in 3NF, which permits a dependency whose right side is prime.

questions.text: Which inference rules follow from Armstrong's axioms?

options.text: If X → Y and X → Z then X → YZ
If X → YZ then X → Y and X → Z
If X → Y and WY → Z then WX → Z
If X → Y then Y → X

questions.solution: A is union, B is decomposition and C is pseudotransitivity, all derivable from the three axioms. D would be a symmetry rule and is false: a student ID determines a name, but names do not determine student IDs.

questions.text: R(A, B, C) has A → B and B → C. How many attributes are in the closure of {A}?
questions.solution: A gives B by the first dependency, and B then gives C, so the closure is ABC. This chain is exactly what transitivity captures: A → C is implied even though it was never written down.

questions.text: Which ACID property guarantees that a transaction either completes entirely or has no effect at all?
questions.solution: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing guarantee, implemented by undoing the partial work of a transaction that fails partway. Durability is the separate promise that a transaction which did commit survives a crash.

questions.text: Which ACID property means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another valid state?
questions.solution: Consistency concerns the integrity constraints — keys, referential integrity, declared checks. It is the one property the application shares responsibility for: the database enforces the constraints it was told about, and the transaction must be written to respect the rest.

questions.text: Isolation guarantees that concurrent execution of transactions is:

options.text: faster than running them one at a time
equivalent to some serial order of those transactions
equivalent to running them in the order they were submitted

questions.solution: The requirement is equivalence to some serial order, not any particular one. Requiring submission order would be far stricter and would forbid most useful concurrency. Isolation says nothing about deadlock, which locking schedulers must handle separately.

questions.text: Which isolation level is required to prevent phantom reads?
questions.solution: A phantom is a row that appears in a repeated range query because another transaction inserted it. REPEATABLE READ protects rows already read but not rows that did not exist yet, so only SERIALIZABLE excludes phantoms.

questions.text: Write-ahead logging requires that:

options.text: the data page reaches disk before its log record
the log record reaches disk before the corresponding data page
log records are written only at commit
the log is kept in memory only

questions.solution: The log must be on disk first, otherwise a crash could leave a modified page with no record of how to undo or redo it. This ordering is what makes both atomicity and durability recoverable after a failure.

questions.text: Which statements about serialisability are TRUE?

options.text: A schedule whose precedence graph is acyclic is conflict-serialisable

questions.solution: Conflict-serialisability is the stricter notion, so A holds and B does not — schedules with blind writes can be view-serialisable without being conflict-serialisable. C is the standard test, and D is true by definition.

questions.text: What is the difference between a superkey and a candidate key?

options.text: A candidate key is a minimal superkey, one with no removable attribute
A superkey must be a single attribute
A candidate key may contain NULLs but a superkey may not

questions.solution: Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row is a superkey. A candidate key is one from which no attribute can be dropped without losing that uniqueness. Every candidate key is a superkey; the reverse fails as soon as you add a spare attribute.

questions.text: Can an attribute of the primary key hold NULL?

options.text: Yes, provided the other attributes are non-NULL
Yes, for at most one row
Only in a composite primary key

questions.solution: This is the entity integrity rule. A NULL means unknown, and an unknown value cannot identify a row. Other candidate keys declared UNIQUE may permit NULLs, depending on the system.

questions.text: A relation has four attributes A, B, C, D, and AB is its only candidate key. How many superkeys does it have?
questions.solution: A superkey is any attribute set containing a candidate key, so every superset of AB qualifies. The remaining attributes C and D may each be in or out, giving 2<sup>2</sup> = 4: AB, ABC, ABD and ABCD.

questions.text: A foreign key in one relation must reference:

options.text: a primary key or candidate key of the referenced relation
a primary key of the same relation

questions.solution: The referenced attributes must identify rows uniquely, otherwise the reference would be ambiguous. A foreign key may point at its own relation, which is how hierarchies such as an employee's manager are modelled.

questions.text: A composite key is:

options.text: a key made of two or more attributes
a key that is also a foreign key
a key generated by the system

questions.solution: Uniqueness comes from the combination, not from any single attribute. A student ID alone may repeat across a course enrolment table, and a course code certainly repeats, but the pair identifies one enrolment.

questions.text: Which statements about candidate keys are TRUE?

options.text: A relation may have more than one candidate key
The candidate keys not chosen as primary are called alternate keys
Every relation has at least one candidate key
A candidate key must be a single attribute

questions.solution: Multiple candidate keys are common — a person may be identified by a national ID or by an email. Those not chosen are alternate keys. C holds because rows in a relation are distinct, so at worst the whole attribute set is a key. D is false: composite candidate keys are ordinary.
